# The Value Premium {#sec-value-replication}

We follow Chapter 10 of @bali2016.
Book-to-market compares an accounting measure of equity with what investors pay for the shares.
We ask how this ratio varies across stocks and whether it predicts the following month's excess return.

## Calculating Book-to-Market Ratio {#calculate-book-to-market}

Book equity in millions is stockholders' equity plus deferred taxes and the investment tax credit, less preferred stock.
We use preferred stock redemption value, liquidation value, or par value, in that order.
BEM require stockholders' equity and deferred taxes.
They use zero for a missing tax credit or when all three preferred stock fields are missing.
We take the last fiscal year-end within the calendar year.

{{< include _show-code.qmd >}}

```{python}
#| include: false

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market
```

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

show_code(build_book_to_market, "funda")
```

Use CRSP–Compustat links valid on the fiscal year-end.
When a direct link is unavailable, try an unambiguous historical CUSIP match.
We use the legacy monthly names file for this fallback.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

show_code(build_book_to_market, "annual_keys", "links", "linked_book", "cusips", "cusip_book", "book")
```

Divide book equity by the nominal December capitalization for the same calendar year, from @sec-size-replication.
Make that ratio available at the end of the following June and carry it through the next May.
This gives a December fiscal year-end at least six months before the ratio enters a portfolio sort.

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| output: asis

show_code(build_book_to_market, "december_cap", "book_to_market")
```

```{python}
import polars as pl

from eap_pl import build_book_to_market, build_sizes

first = pl.date(1963, 6, 1)
last = pl.date(2012, 11, 1)
keys = ["permno", "month"]

all_sizes = build_sizes()
book_to_market = build_book_to_market(all_sizes)
```

For this chapter, use positive book equity so the logarithm is defined.
The table also keeps the signed ratio for the annual summaries in @sec-summary-characteristics.

```{python}
#| include: false

import os

from eap_pl import write_eap_table

assert book_to_market.select(pl.struct(keys).n_unique()).item() == book_to_market.height
if os.environ.get("EAP_WRITE_BOOK_TO_MARKET") == "1":
    write_eap_table(book_to_market, "book_to_market")

sizes = all_sizes.filter(
    pl.col("common"), pl.col("month").is_between(first, last)
)
```

## Summary Statistics

The numerator and denominator come from the same annual vintage.
For the dollar amounts in the table, express both in December 2012 dollars using the CPI for the observation month.
The common deflator leaves the book-to-market ratio unchanged.

{{< include _show-table.qmd >}}

```{python}
from eap_pl import mean_cross_sections, monthly_panel

panel = monthly_panel(sizes, first, last).join(book_to_market, on=keys, how="left", validate="1:1")
cpi = pl.read_csv("data/cpi-aucns.csv", try_parse_dates=True).rename(
    {"observation_date": "month", "CPIAUCNS": "cpi"}
)
cpi_2012 = cpi.filter(pl.col("month") == pl.date(2012, 12, 1))["cpi"].item()
value_panel = (
    panel.filter(pl.col("bm").is_not_null())
    .join(cpi, on="month", validate="m:1")
    .with_columns(
        be_real=pl.col("be") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
        me_real=pl.col("me") * cpi_2012 / pl.col("cpi"),
    )
)
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-summary
#| tbl-cap: Monthly summary statistics for book-to-market (BEM Table 10.1)
#| echo: false

show_table(mean_cross_sections(value_panel, {
    "bm": "BM", "log_bm": "ln BM", "be_real": "Book equity",
    "me_real": "December market equity", "cap": "Current market cap",
}))
```

Availability depends on finding both a fiscal book value and a prior December capitalization.

## Correlations {#correlation-and-persistence}

The Pearson correlations use 0.5% winsorization at both ends of each pair's monthly sample.
The Spearman correlations use the original ranks.
Since the logarithm preserves order for positive ratios, BM and ln BM have a Spearman correlation of one and the same rank correlation with each other variable.

```{python}
from eap_pl import correlation_matrix, period_correlations, persistence

measures = {"bm": "BM", "log_bm": "ln BM", "beta": "Beta", "log_cap": "Size"}
corr = period_correlations(value_panel, measures, "month").select(pl.exclude("month").mean())
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-correlations
#| tbl-cap: Monthly cross-sectional correlations with book-to-market (BEM Table 10.2)
#| echo: false
show_table(correlation_matrix(corr.row(0, named=True), measures))
```

## Persistence

Book-to-market updates once a year, so we start the persistence analysis at a lag of twelve months.
Shorter lags would often compare the same book-to-market observation with itself.
As in the annual persistence analysis, winsorize each side after matching the sample by date and stock.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-persistence
#| tbl-cap: Persistence of book-to-market (BEM Table 10.3)
#| echo: false
show_table(persistence(value_panel, {"bm": "BM", "log_bm": "ln BM"}, [12, 24, 36, 48, 60, 120]))
```

## Book-to-Market Ratio and Stock Returns {#book-to-market-and-future-returns}

### Univariate Portfolio Analysis

Form ten portfolios at the end of each month using the book-to-market ratio.
Compare breakpoints from all eligible stocks with breakpoints from NYSE stocks.
Holding returns use the next month's CRSP returns and the delisting adjustment in @sec-bem-returns.
Value weights use current market capitalization at formation.
Returns and CAPM alphas are percentages per month, and $t$-statistics use six Newey–West lags.

```{python}
from eap_pl import bivariate_months, bivariate_panel, fama_macbeth_table, univariate_panel

characteristics = [
    pl.col("bm").mean().alias("BM"), pl.col("log_bm").mean().alias("ln BM"),
    pl.col("cap").mean().alias("Market cap"), pl.col("beta").mean().alias("Beta"),
    (100 * (pl.col("exchcd") == 1).fill_null(False).mean()).alias("% NYSE"),
    pl.len().alias("Stocks"),
]
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-deciles
#| tbl-cap: Book-to-market deciles with all-stock and NYSE breakpoints (BEM Table 10.4)
#| echo: false
show_table(pl.concat([
    univariate_panel(value_panel, "bm", nyse, characteristics)
    .with_columns(pl.lit(label).alias("Breakpoints"))
    for nyse, label in [(False, "All stocks"), (True, "NYSE")]
]).select("Breakpoints", pl.exclude("Breakpoints")))
```

With all-stock breakpoints, the high-minus-low spread is 1.33% per month with equal weights and 0.57% with value weights.

### Bivariate Portfolio Analysis {#control-for-beta-or-size}

Sort first on a control variable, then on book-to-market within each control quintile.
This asks whether the return difference between high and low book-to-market stocks persists among stocks of similar beta or size.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-dependent
#| tbl-cap: Dependent book-to-market sorts controlling for beta or size (BEM Table 10.5)
#| echo: false

average_portfolios, differences = [], []
for control, label in [("beta", "Beta"), ("cap", "Market cap")]:
    portfolios = bivariate_months(panel, control, "bm", nyse=False, dependent=True)
    for weight in ("EW", "VW"):
        averages, spreads = bivariate_panel(portfolios, weight, independent=False, spread_only=True)
        average_portfolios.append(averages.rename({"Target": "Portfolio"}).with_columns(
            pl.lit("Across control quintiles").alias("Panel"),
            pl.lit(label).alias("Sort"), pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"),
        ))
        differences.append(spreads.rename({
            "Control": "Portfolio", "5–1 excess return": "Excess return", "5–1 CAPM alpha": "CAPM alpha",
        }).with_columns(
            pl.lit("BM 5–1 within control quintile").alias("Panel"),
            pl.lit(label).alias("Sort"), pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"),
        ))
show_table(pl.concat(differences + average_portfolios).select(
    "Panel", "Sort", "Weights", "Portfolio", "Excess return", "CAPM alpha",
))
```

With independent sorts, the book-to-market cutoffs are the same in each control quintile.
Each portfolio is the intersection of the two quintile assignments.
An average portfolio equally weights the five constituent portfolio returns each month.

```{python}
def value_quintiles(control):
    portfolios = bivariate_months(panel, control, "bm", nyse=False, dependent=False)
    return pl.concat([
        bivariate_panel(portfolios, weight, independent=True)
        .with_columns(pl.lit(weight).alias("Weights"))
        for weight in ("EW", "VW")
    ]).select("Weights", pl.exclude("Weights")).rename({"Target": "BM"})
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-independent-beta
#| tbl-cap: Independent book-to-market and beta sorts (BEM Table 10.6)
#| echo: false
show_table(value_quintiles("beta"))
```

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-independent-size
#| tbl-cap: Independent book-to-market and size sorts (BEM Table 10.7)
#| echo: false
show_table(value_quintiles("cap"))
```

### Fama–MacBeth Regression Analysis {#famamacbeth-regressions}

Compare the slopes on raw and logged book-to-market with and without beta and log size.
The explanatory variables are winsorized within month at the 0.5th and 99.5th percentiles.

```{python}
#| label: tbl-bem10-fm
#| tbl-cap: Fama–MacBeth regressions of returns on book-to-market (BEM Table 10.8)
#| echo: false

specifications = [
    [measure, *controls]
    for measure in ["bm", "log_bm"]
    for controls in [[], ["beta"], ["log_cap"], ["beta", "log_cap"]]
]
show_table(fama_macbeth_table(panel, specifications, measures))
```

## The Value Factor

HML averages the high-book-to-market portfolios across the two size groups and subtracts the average of their low-book-to-market counterparts.
Using small and big stocks on both sides reduces the weight of the size effect in the comparison.
We use the published monthly Fama–French HML series from July 1926 through December 2012.

```{python}
#| label: fig-bem10-hml
#| fig-cap: Cumulative returns on the Fama–French HML factor (BEM Figure 10.1)
#| echo: false
from eap_pl import plot_factor

plot_factor("hml")
```

In the Fama–French three-factor model, the intercept measures the portfolio's return after accounting for exposures to market, size, and value factors.
For excess portfolio return $r_{p,t}$, the regression is

$$
r_{p,t}=\alpha_p+\beta_{p,M}MKT_t+\beta_{p,S}SMB_t+\beta_{p,H}HML_t+\varepsilon_{p,t}.
$$
